title: Higher-for-Longer Cemented as the Fed Hikes and the Global Long End Sells Off
content:
Higher-for-longer became the window's through-line. The Fed delivered a 25bp hike to **3.75%-4%** on 16 September in a 12-0 vote — its first rise since 2023 — with the dot plot pointing to another move in December while core PCE held above 3% for every month of the year.

The sharper action, though, was at the long end, where a global rout drove the US 10-year near **5.16%** and the 30-year to roughly **5.48%**, their highest since 2007 and 2004. Investors argued over whether sticky inflation, resilient growth or swelling deficits was to blame, but the common thread was a rising **term premium** that lifted yields worldwide.

Higher long rates raised discount rates across equities, housing and credit, firmed the dollar and left markets braced for something to break. Auction demand and the December decision remained the swing factors.

title: US-Iran Conflict and Strait of Hormuz Threats Keep Crude Elevated
content:
A persistent Middle East **supply shock** ran through the window as the US-Iran war escalated in the Persian Gulf and threats to the Strait of Hormuz — the world's most important oil chokepoint — kept a risk premium embedded in crude.

Prices stayed volatile and elevated. Brent traded around **$106** by 25 September after jumping more than 3% on reports of fresh attacks earlier in the month, with WTI in the high-90s. Tehran's conditional offer to reopen Hormuz and resume nuclear talks injected two-way risk, yet regional energy flows remained disrupted.

The shock mattered because elevated energy fed directly into inflation prints and hawkish central-bank rhetoric, reinforcing the higher-for-longer rates story. Any renewed Hormuz closure stayed the key upside tail for prices — and the main downside tail for global risk assets.

title: Gold's Record Run Extends as a Debasement and Safe-Haven Hedge
content:
Gold's climb to fresh record highs became a defining cross-asset trend and the window's clearest new signal. Bullion pushed above **$4,500** intraday and held near record levels into late September, extending a run of more than **25%** since early 2025.

The move was striking because it persisted despite a firm dollar and surging real yields, normally stiff headwinds for a non-yielding asset. Instead, record ETF demand — global holdings hit an all-time high after roughly **$18bn** of August inflows — alongside steady central-bank buying pointed to a structural bid.

The rally read as a **debasement hedge** against heavy fiscal deficits, sticky inflation and geopolitical risk, offering diversification as both bonds and equities wobbled. Gold's resilience to high real rates made its momentum a closely watched gauge of underlying investor anxiety.

title: AI Megacap Concentration Meets Rising Discount Rates
content:
Equity leadership stayed narrowly tethered to the AI complex, leaving benchmarks hostage to a handful of megacaps just as rising yields pressured the richest valuations. **Narrow breadth** left indices unusually exposed to single-name swings.

The fault line widened on 14 September, when the PHLX Semiconductor Index fell **5.9%**, Nvidia dropped **3.4%** and Micron lost more than 5%, even as software diverged — Meta jumped nearly **13%** on the week on enthusiasm for its new AI agent. The S&P 500 still ground back toward records near **7,743**.

The split questioned the AI trade's single-engine dominance precisely as discount rates climbed, sharpening the test of whether AI earnings can justify stretched valuations against a tightening Fed. With megacaps steering direction, their durability became the market's central Q4 question.
